speechtext: The proposals known as federal union or "Union Now". I am not going into all the details, but in substance they believe in a world currency based on gold; in an international police force, which is the maintenance of a standing army and navy under the control of one central power, and in a world judiciary. Put that trinity of evil together and what chance has a small nation to exercise its own God-given democratic rights?

maintopic: POST-WAR RECONSTRUCTION APPOINTMENT OF SELECT COMMITTEE ON RECONSTRUCTION AND REESTABLISHMENT
speechtext: What chance has it now?

maintopic: POST-WAR RECONSTRUCTION APPOINTMENT OF SELECT COMMITTEE ON RECONSTRUCTION AND REESTABLISHMENT
speechtext:
It has no chance now. We are fighting against a tremendous military power that is attempting eventually to rule the world. We want to defeat that power and maintain our own democratic rights. Underlying this there is another power just as vicious, a centralized power, seeking to rob us of our democratic rights. As the nazi power is attempting to do it by military force, the other power will attempt to do by an international banking conspiracy. That is the position, and while we may win on the one hand we may lose on -the other.
All I am saying is that the committee should go into these matters in minutest detail. We have as chairman of the seven-man committee of the government a man who we have reason to believe is very nearly an exponent of the proposals of that same "Union Now". I refer to Doctor James, principal of McGill university, who on one occasion ran off to Washington and who I believe is now in England. When the hon member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) last week brought that to the attention of the Minister of Pensions and National Health the minister said he could tell the house that Doctor James was not running this government. Those words were sweet music to my ears. Nevertheless Doctor James is chairman of that committee, and I say that the proposed committee of the house should have the right to call Doctor James to the stand, put him under oath and keep a record of what he says so that we can learn exactly what is going on behind the scenes.
Canada is in an excellent position to give leadership in connection with post-war reconstruction, and in particular to tell the world 
right now that we will not stand for this government or this country being taken back into a system based upon gold and controlled internationally. I say Canada is in an ideal position to do that, because in spite of criticism one way or another, Canada is playing a vital role in the present world conflict. We are supplying Great Britain with vast quantities of munitions and supplies, and we have reason to believe that we are of tremendous help to the United States of America. Just last night we gave second reading to a bill to give Great Britain one billion dollars this year with which to buy 'Canadian production. Canada therefore is playing an important part in the present world conflict and is in an excellent position to give leadership in this whole matter of world reconstruction.
There is another question I should like to deal with for a moment. I have forgotten the exact words used by the hon. member for Vancouver' East (Mr. Maclnnis) as he rose just now, but in sum and substance I think he said that the danger is that the people do not see far enough ahead. That perhaps touches the crux of the whole situation with respect to movements that are taking place in the world, including Canada. I have always said, and I think hon. members will agree, that strong leadership is leadership that will lead and not follow. In order to lead, a leadership must inform the public so that'an informed public will go step by step with them. But the fact is that things are put over on the public. I am fearful that in our post-war reconstruction the very thing I have protested against will again be imposed upon the public.
I am anxious to see the present government and the government that will be in power when the war ends give outstanding leadership in the reconstruction of the post-war world. In order to do that they must have the people with them. In order to have the people with them the people must be informed. Facilities should be made available to inform the public on every phase of an issue. I am not going to say I should be satisfied with simply printing a report of the committee's proceedings; I suggest that the widest publicity be given to it, and equal publicity to every phase of post-war reconstruction, so that the people may be informed of the benefits of one thing and the dangers of another.
I had intended to speak on this matter at some length. The motion, however, was brought down rather suddenly. It was given the usual notice in the Votes and Proceedings, of course, but as the leader of the opposition has already said, if we had a little more time on this matter I think the house itself would

Post-War Reconstruction
have gone to some length in its discussion of post-war reconstruction. You see what is happening now. Here is a motion to set up a committee. If we want to talk on post-war reconstruction, we had better do it now. When this motion passes the committee is set up, and then everything will be done by the committee. Reports will be made to the house, but if my prognosis is correct a motion for concurrence in the reports of the committee will not be mad^, so that there will be no opportunity to discuss these matters unless we do so on some general topic. Do I understand that the minister has promised the house that time will be given for adequate discussion when the reports of the committee come up in the house?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: POST-WAR RECONSTRUCTION APPOINTMENT OF SELECT COMMITTEE ON RECONSTRUCTION AND REESTABLISHMENT
speechtext: Certainly.

maintopic: POST-WAR RECONSTRUCTION APPOINTMENT OF SELECT COMMITTEE ON RECONSTRUCTION AND REESTABLISHMENT
speechtext: That is music to my ears, too, Mr. Speaker, because it is my profound conviction that if the fundamental evils of our entire system are not corrected, we shall not solve our problems after the war is won.

maintopic: POST-WAR RECONSTRUCTION APPOINTMENT OF SELECT COMMITTEE ON RECONSTRUCTION AND REESTABLISHMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I just want to support the view of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson), that a full statement of what the government has already done, and perhaps what it has in mind, should be made before this committee is set up or this matter sent to the committee.
I do not intend to prolong the debate; there is a great deal of important business to be done, but I do want to impress upon the minister my support of the suggestion of the leader of the opposition that before this committee is set up and this subject matter referred to it, the minister should make a full and complete statement to this house in order that we may know what has been done and thus be prepared to discuss the question later. I may add that to no other group in the house is the appointment of this committee a matter of greater satisfaction than it is to us, but we would appreciate a full statement by the minister before the reference to the committee of the subject matter of the resolution.

maintopic: POST-WAR RECONSTRUCTION APPOINTMENT OF SELECT COMMITTEE ON RECONSTRUCTION AND REESTABLISHMENT
speechtext:
I notice, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member for Danforth is to be on this committee. I remember the magnitude of the problem along these lines, in connection with reconstruction and rehabilitation, that had to be faced at the end of the last war. I remember that those who at present occupy the treasury benches made very strong representations across Canada that sufficient was not being done, and later made many promises as to what would be done, for those who were returning from world war No. 1. So much
was this propaganda spread across Canada that after the election of 1921 hon. gentlemen found themselves in power. Since that time I cannot remember having the honour and privilege of serving on any committee dealing with these questions until after a statement had been made to this house as to the detail of what the committee was being set up for, and what the ideas were in the mind of the minister in charge.
At the present time we have a very able minister in charge of this department, whose responsibility it is to keep up to the minute on every phase of this very important subject matter. No one in this chamber is better qualified than the minister to give a lead to hon. members as to what might or what ought to be done. I realize that we are anxious to approach this problem from a non-partisan point of view, but we must have some starting point. During the days when hon. gentlemen opposite occupied the benches which we at present occupy, I think perhaps not only the minister but also the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) will remember their anxiety that we should have responsible government in Canada by a responsible administration. To my mind the very essence of responsible government is that in connection with a matter of this kind the government charged with responsibility shall give the house its policy.
It may be said that the war is still going on, and that this policy cannot be properly enunciated now. That may be quite true, but we should like to know what has happened during the last ten years. Would it not be possible for the minister to bring us up to date as to what facilities will be available when the time comes? All this information- is in the department, but in fairness to this house we should be told, before this committee is convened. The minister must give us some lead. Of course that will not be final, because the war is not over. It will be amended first by the members of this committee, when they have the benefit of the presentations that will be made by those appearing before them. But at least we should be brought up to date and should not be sent out into the wilderness without knowing where we are going or whether we are right or wrong. Then as one year follows another the policy can be further amended, following further declarations by the minister.
If the minister does not make a statement on these matters now I should say he has failed in his duty in connection with the introduction of this resolution. We are all
Post-War Reconstruction

anxious as to what will happen when this tragedy of war is over, with regard to those who will return. That is the first point. We are anxious too with regard to those who now find themselves in profitable employment, and we are concerned with those who are dependent upon the first two groups I have mentioned. If a statement is made by the minister now, the morale of Canadians in all three groups will be greatly strengthened. They will know that we are about to consider the matter, and they will know that a responsible minister has given some lead. But if we set up a committee and start on a fishing expedition as to what might be done, we may be submerged by all kinds of hare-brained ideas coming from all sections of the country, and we may fritter away our time looking into matters which no doubt already have come to the attention of the minister in his study of this reconstruction problem. On the other hand if we had the considered opinion of the government as to what might be done, and were assured that all the frills and fads were eliminated, we could give our attention to the very kernel of the problem. We could bring back an up-to-the-minute report, so that the country would know that this matter had had careful and sound consideration. In the other case we go before a committee and wander from one thought to. another, or one subject to another without having governmental responsibility as a basis. I strongly urge upon the minister that he give consideration to the thought expressed by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) and, as I gather, approved by hon. members sitting to our left.

maintopic: POST-WAR RECONSTRUCTION APPOINTMENT OF SELECT COMMITTEE ON RECONSTRUCTION AND REESTABLISHMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, next to the measures directly related to the carrying on of the war, this is, in my opinion, the most important measure to come before the house at this session. Like other hon. members, I had not expected it would be reached before the recess, but I take this opportunity of placing before the house as briefly as possible, without preparation, one or two views on the matter.
I wish to emphasize with all the strength of my being the importance of the resolution and of the work the committee will undertake. Next to winning the war, or to any measure directly connected with that undertaking, we could not spend our time in any more profitable way. I am glad that hon. members have refrained from saying, as some newspapers have said, "Let's get on with the war, and postpone any talk about post-war matters until the war is over." Unless we talk about 
post-war matters during the war, we may not have a post-war world. I would be the first to say that we ought not to spend a minute on this discussion if I thought that by continuing it we were postponing the making of a single shell. On the other hand I believe that discussion such as we are having to-day, and the work of the committee which will flow from it, will make us fight better. It will give us something more positive than we have yet had to fight for.
We can base the emotions which direct and charge us in fighting this war on hate, or we can base them on the hope that something better will come from victory. My belief is that our war effort will be far stronger and far better than the enemy's if we do not follow the line of hate, but rather choose the line of hope and work for the realization of that hope during as well as after the war. I believe that our people will fight better, that they will give their blood, and their sweat and their tears more freely if they believe that in consequence of what they are giving they will not return to periods of scarcity and unemployment, but have some reasonable expectation of attaining better conditions than we have known before.
This subject is being discussed everywhere throughout the world, both on our side and on that of the enemy. Hitler has laid out his plan of a new world order, and one of the great motivating forces impelling his armies, so far so successfully, is the hope that that new world order will be realized. Hitler has used the forces of propaganda and ideas to fight for him. We have better ideas than he has. We have a better system of government, and we have a better civilization; otherwise we would not be fighting at all. But in the past we have stopped short of making our ideals fight for us, as they should.
Everywhere among the allied nations I find that discussions of this kind are going on. I spent the week-end attending an exceedingly interesting conference at Williamstown, under the auspices of Williams college. To that conference men came from all parts of the eastern United States to discuss this subject. The consensus of those men, experts in their various fields, was that in order to have the united nations make their utmost effort it was necessary to clothe the bare bones of the declaration of those nations with something more positive than we yet have had. There was the feeling that the united nations must have common ideals for which they are fighting. Up to the present we have not made our union effective; we are fighting separate wars rather than one war. This is a global

Post-War Reconstruction
war. We are fighting Hitler and the forces of the axis powers everywhere, and one front is as important as another.
With respect to the post-war objective of the work of the committee I should like to say one or two words. I do not think anyone has yet realized the magnitude of the job which will face the government of the day that will deal with the post-war problem. If we stopped the war to-day we would have 10 per cent of our population directly engaged either in the active fighting forces or in the making of munitions. Would their work stop? Would they become unemployed? What machinery would be provided? What controls, what construction projects would be necessary to provide employment for that 10 per cent of the population, until our economy began to function properly again? This can be judged by a single figure. In 1942 the nations of the world will make 150,000 aeroplanes. In 1939, to supply the commercial airways of the entire world with normal replacements and additions, 250 planes were required. The difference between those figures is some indication of the magnitude of the post-war problem, from the point of view of employment of war workers alone.
Then, let us consider it from the point of view of the constitution of Canada. At the end of the last war two cases were decided by the privy council which held that the government's power under the War Measures Act ceased with the termination of hostilities. If those decisions were to be followed at the conclusion of this war, the government would not be able to do any of the things which ought to be done to carry on the life of the country with the controls and powers it exercises through the War Measures Act. So consideration should be given by the committee-and I hope later by the government- to the constitutional questions involved.
Perhaps we may decide-I hope so-to build half a million houses in Canada within five years after the war. We cannot have a housing project of that nature unless it is done as a national enterprise, and with nation-wide powers. So I suggest that here is a field of study which the committee might properly take up in the course of its work.
The problem of unemployment must somehow be licked. Everyone has known for years that the world can produce enough food and necessities for every man, woman and child-brown, black, white and red1-on its surface. But we have not learned the technique of production and distribution well, enough, particularly distribution. To-day the working forces of the world are at work.
In Canada they see the full dinner-pail for everyone at a time when we are engaged in manufacturing things to be used for destruction. We see that happening in Canada at a time when we are reducing our external debt and giving to Britain more than twice as much as we ever sold her in any year before, and people are asking themselves: If that is possible in war, why not in peace? That question is going to be a very difficult one to answer unless the answer is: Yes, we can and we will do it. That is a simple question to the men overseas and the workmen in the factories of Canada. It is going to require complicated answers to show that it is not possible or that it should not be done. I suggest that we must strive to reach the stage after the war where there will be virtual full employment, or governments will go.
Everywhere we see under consideration plans, internal and external, to provide the maximum amount of employment. An exceedingly interesting book has just been issued by Alvin Hansen, the American economist, on precisely that subject. He believes that full employment can be obtained in the United States and that it would be the greatest contribution by the United States to post-war settlement. Measures to provide maximum employment are under consideration everywhere, but it is obvious that it cannot be done by any nation alone. That we have to cooperate is just as evident as that day follows night.
I am completely with my friend in the southeast corner when he said that freedom from want and freedom from fear are two objectives which must be realized, and I certainly agree with him in his remarks about the plan, "Union Now". On the other hand, I say that what we want has to be done by a combination of external and internal measures, springing from a realization for the first time by the nations of the world that they are interdependent and that the world is one, and by their beginning to tackle problems which they can face together but which they cannot face alone.
I suggest that if it is possible the proposed committee should secure the views of outstanding people from other countries. It is of the utmost importance that in this matter we make sure that our thinking in Canada takes account of the thinking in other parts of the world-in Britain, where there has been a great deal of work done, in the United States, and in the British dominions and the countries of the united nations. I suggest that that study can be carried on effectively only if it is carried on in close correspondence with our opposite numbers in other countries of the
Post-War Reconstruction

world so as to make sure that we are beginning to think about the same things at the same time and beginning to decide on similar lines of policy that must be followed if success is to be achieved.
Finally, may I say that in the plan of a postwar world or post-war reconstruction I do not think any blueprint can be laid out in detail now. What can be done is to see the nature of the problem, consider its magnitude, consider the kind of objectives that must be worked for and the kind of means that must be followed, and then gradually set up the machinery by which the transfer from a war to a peace economy is to be effected.
We are fighting in this war for survival. We are not fighting for anything else at the moment. We are fighting to defeat Hitler. Victory is a prerequisite to lfe. Life would not be worth while without it. But victory will not give us any more than a chance. Having achieved it, all it gives us is a new start. We shall have a chance of avoiding the mistakes we made after the last war. We have had twenty years of experience, of development in understanding, to guide us. But it will be hopeless if suddenly the war comes to an end and peace comes on us and catches us unprepared. It will produce nothing but chaos in our thinking and chaos in our organization. We may then have a call for a khaki election and for this and that. We shall fail to serve our best interests unless we are prepared and the people are prepared by thinking of these problems now. To have a khaki election might have results as disastrous as the khaki election in Britain after the last war and after the south African war, two elections which produced perhaps the two worst governments that country ever had.
The problem is imminent. We have been at war for two and a half years. I dare say that everyone in this chamber hopes, although it is not certain, that we may have victory within another two and a half years; but if we have done no more in the next two years than we have been able to do in the past to prepare for peace, victory and peace will catch us unprepared, and we shall then have to pay the penalty of our unpreparedness.
In order to make our utmost effort, Canada along with the united nations must have faith that, in consequence of that effort being made, we shall get, not only victory, but the chance to work for a better world than we have ever had before an-d the probability that we are going to get it. But to achieve this, the united nations and the peoples of each of the United Nations must share their views and ideas, create habits of thinking together, build confidence in each other and in their ability to carry out their purposes.

Our aim to defeat the enemy is only a stage. The need for a united will and united action goes far beyond victory. We must see that the four freedoms which President Roosevelt defined for the world belong to us and to our children, the children of Canada, and children everywhere in the world.

maintopic: POST-WAR RECONSTRUCTION APPOINTMENT OF SELECT COMMITTEE ON RECONSTRUCTION AND REESTABLISHMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I notice that I am a member of the proposed committee. But first I want to say that the busiest time I have in this house is when I am trying to decide whether something I have to say is relevant to the matter under discussion. Many times I have risen to say something which I have considered important and intended to state briefly, only to be declared out of order. Most of the discussion that has taken place here this afternoon I consider a waste of time, and being Scotch, I do not like a waste of time. The Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie), following the discussions which have taken place on this subject in the house for the past two years and a half, has brought in a resolution to set up a committee to study the subject matter of those speeches. The committee that has been set up will, in my opinion, have very little to do with settling these questions, because my understanding is that there has already been a committee studying this problem for the past two years, and that the committee now being set up here under this resolution is merely instructed to study and report to the house on reconstruction and reestablishment after the war. The committee has no authority to do anything except gather information and pass that information on to another committee, which, in the final analysis, will decide what is going to be done about this problem. That is my understanding of the appointment, of this committee, and I think we might very well adopt this resolution without further discussion, because frankly I am not hearing anything this afternoon that I have not been listening to for the past two years.
I rose particularly to ask the Minister of Pensions and National Health whether the committee which had been studying this problem for. the past two and a half years has complete and final say in the matter of rehabilitation.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: POST-WAR RECONSTRUCTION APPOINTMENT OF SELECT COMMITTEE ON RECONSTRUCTION AND REESTABLISHMENT
speechtext: Absolutely not. Their only function is to make recommendations in regard to procedure with reference to future policies to be adopted. They have no authority whatsoever.

maintopic: POST-WAR RECONSTRUCTION APPOINTMENT OF SELECT COMMITTEE ON RECONSTRUCTION AND REESTABLISHMENT
speechtext:
And this select committee is to be appointed for the purpose of gathering

Post-War Reconstruction
information and passing it on to the smaller committee, which in turn will boil it down and make recommendations to the government?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: POST-WAR RECONSTRUCTION APPOINTMENT OF SELECT COMMITTEE ON RECONSTRUCTION AND REESTABLISHMENT
speechtext: May I explain to my hon. friend? Last year, at the request of many members of this house we had a committee on soldiers' rehabilitation, of which my hon. friend was a very able member. Immediately we met we called in to give evidence the committees which had been working under my direction for some twelve or fourteen months, so that the parliamentary committee of this house might be made thoroughly familiar with all the progress which had been made in the meantime by the interdepartmental committees which had been studying these various problems. I would imagine that exactly the same procedure would be followed in the present instance.

maintopic: POST-WAR RECONSTRUCTION APPOINTMENT OF SELECT COMMITTEE ON RECONSTRUCTION AND REESTABLISHMENT
speechtext: The only difference I see is that the committee on pensions drafted their own report. They boiled down the evidence submitted and tabled in the house their own report. My understanding of this committee is that they will not do that-

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: POST-WAR RECONSTRUCTION APPOINTMENT OF SELECT COMMITTEE ON RECONSTRUCTION AND REESTABLISHMENT
speechtext: Oh, yes. Certainly.

maintopic: POST-WAR RECONSTRUCTION APPOINTMENT OF SELECT COMMITTEE ON RECONSTRUCTION AND REESTABLISHMENT
speechtext: -that they will merely report to the cabinet committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: POST-WAR RECONSTRUCTION APPOINTMENT OF SELECT COMMITTEE ON RECONSTRUCTION AND REESTABLISHMENT
speechtext: No. They will report to this house.

maintopic: POST-WAR RECONSTRUCTION APPOINTMENT OF SELECT COMMITTEE ON RECONSTRUCTION AND REESTABLISHMENT
speechtext:
I should like to have an understanding of this question of when one is in order and when not in order. I do not care if we discuss this question of rehabilitation for the next year. The hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris) warns us of what may happen if we do not do what we did after the last war. Let me say that if we do not do more than that, personally I do not want to be living in this country when the army that is overseas comes back.
I do not agree with the statement that hon. members are not getting enough work, and I have no wish to sit on a committee merely to make an addition to my work; that is not a sufficient reason. I have more work now than I can do. But I consider this is the most important job I can go on. As a member of that committee I am not going there to waste time. If any hon. member outside the committee has definite views on the subject and wishes to present them, I personally should be pleased to hear him, and will use what I learn to the best advantage.
The terms of reference in this resolution are very broad, and as far as I am concerned I am going to make full use of the latitude it allows.

maintopic: POST-WAR RECONSTRUCTION APPOINTMENT OF SELECT COMMITTEE ON RECONSTRUCTION AND REESTABLISHMENT
speechtext: Has this committee power to arrange for service clubs in the municipalities, manufacturers, and others, to list jobs which can be done after the war?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: POST-WAR RECONSTRUCTION APPOINTMENT OF SELECT COMMITTEE ON RECONSTRUCTION AND REESTABLISHMENT
speechtext: Yes. As a matter of fact, that work is now being done by one of the subcommittees.

maintopic: POST-WAR RECONSTRUCTION APPOINTMENT OF SELECT COMMITTEE ON RECONSTRUCTION AND REESTABLISHMENT
speechtext:
I am veiy happy to see my name on the committee, because during the past few years I have been making an exhaustive study of this question, mostly in the direction of a survey of public resources. In the course of much travel I have found that vast resources in this country are tied up, and have been for many years, by interests of one kind or another. I have in mind a very large area said to contain hundreds of millions of tons of high-grade coal. Upon making inquiries why no coal was being mined, I was informed that the property belonged to a certain estate, which had held it for many years. I hope the time will come when this country will forbid the retention of unworked natural resources by private interests beyond a reasonable length of time.
I do not believe that they should be permitted to profit to the extent of millions of dollars because other properties in the neighbourhood have been developed in the meanwhile. Another example which occurs to me is a site not many miles east of Ottawa, and well known to most hon. members, where from a million and a half to two million horse-power can be developed, should have been developed, and should now be in use for the production of munitions with which to fight this war; yet there are no signs of development. I hope the committee will not be precluded from recommending the development of such national resources. When the government of Canada or of any province gives such rights to private individuals, there should be inserted in the contract a time limit within which the resources shall be utilized; otherwise they shall revert to the crown.
Mr. NORMAN J. M. LOCKHART (Lincoln): May I also add a word, more in the form of an interrogation of the minister? It is evident, both from the minister's brief statement and from the information in the hands of hon. members, that considerable inquiry has been made into this problem, particularly during the past two years. The minister has said that he is going to make
Post-War Reconstruction

a statement to the committee and not to this house. May I ask him whether, with all the information which has been gleaned JP to the present, the government is not now in a position to make some definite statement as to its policy of reconstruction after the war, so that when the committee retires at Easter all hon. members will be in a position to direct in some way the deliberations of the committee after the recess? I should like to know why that statement has to be deferred. Is it because the government has as yet no policy for reconstruction which it can submit to the house, and, instead of giving leadership, is looking for further light before enunciating some policy? I do not want the minister to assume that my criticism is biased by political considerations, but it is a fact that back home the people are asking the question; returned men of the last war, too, are asking the question, and we are, so to speak, wandering in the wilderness if we do not get something definite to work on. It seems to me that the government has had sufficient opportunity to give some light to the committee, and that other hon. members should have something which they can pass on during the Easter recess.

maintopic: POST-WAR RECONSTRUCTION APPOINTMENT OF SELECT COMMITTEE ON RECONSTRUCTION AND REESTABLISHMENT
speechtext:
I am in agreement with the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) when he says that he thinks a lot of this discussion should take place in committee; but, since this resolution is almost identical in substance with that of a motion which is on the order paper in my name, I would ask permission of the house to withdraw my motion at this time.
I would also draw to the attention of members of the committee that it has to deal with reconstruction, and its assignment to the study of reconstruction implies that something in the past has failed and that we are to build something new. Proposals to reestablish parts of an old system which have failed will not receive very kindly consideration.
As a member of this committee, I shall work with everything I can to contribute something, in the hope that it will prove of more value than some of the promises which have been passed out from this house in the past. I wish it good luck.

maintopic: POST-WAR RECONSTRUCTION APPOINTMENT OF SELECT COMMITTEE ON RECONSTRUCTION AND REESTABLISHMENT
speechtext:
As a member of the banking and commerce committee of 1939 I suggest to the house that there was at that time an interesting discussion in regard to banking in Canada, the mechanics of financing and so forth, and it might be useful if tlhe banking committee were given some 
information with respect to the present-day financing of Canada so that the public might understand what is going on and what the prospects are for financing in the future. Information could be obtained1 by the banking committee which would be very useful to the reconstruction committee. I suggest that there .might be some meetings of the banking committee, such as we (had in 1939, and I would also commend to hon. members, as very interesting reading, the summary of the report of the banking committee of that day.
Hon. IAN A. MACKENZIE (Vancouver Centre): I am rather surprised at the -way in which this debate has developed -this afternoon. Especially am I surprised at the remarks of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson). Looking at Hansard of March 5 of the present session, I find that my hon. friend specifically asked this house to set up such a committee as is now being organized for the purposes which are outlined in the language of the resolution. A similar request came also from the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell).

maintopic: POST-WAR RECONSTRUCTION APPOINTMENT OF SELECT COMMITTEE ON RECONSTRUCTION AND REESTABLISHMENT
speechtext: Not quite in the same form.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: POST-WAR RECONSTRUCTION APPOINTMENT OF SELECT COMMITTEE ON RECONSTRUCTION AND REESTABLISHMENT
speechtext:
Probably not. It came, too, from several other members of the house. Hon. members will recall a resolution which appeared on the order paper in 1940, placed there by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), which was withdrawn with the unanimous consent of the house because of the tragic war episodes of those days.
I have refrained from taking up more of the time of the house this afternoon in describing in detail all the ivorkings of the reconstruction committee of last year. I had an address ready which I could have given. I appreciate as strongly as any member of the house the importance of devoting attention to post-war reconstruction, but I agree with the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green), who said last night that there is something more urgent just now in Canada than post-war problems, and that is guaranteeing that thing without which reconstruction will never be possible, namely, the winning of the war to ensure victory for our arms and our cause.
The first essential of reconstruction is the attainment of victory, because if we do not win the war, if we do not bend all our efforts and energies toward that end, we shall all be reconstructed by someone else. On the other hand, I agree that there is nothing, next to the winning of the war, which is more important

Privilege-Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury)
than a planned and careful study of the problems of the aftermath. They are giving attention to this question in the United Kingdom and they are doing the same in the United States. I have been in touch with the organizations in those countries. We are exchanging correspondence with the committees concerned, and I venture to say that just as we are to-day the most advanced country in the world from the point of view of legislation which we have already passed with reference to our service men in the present war, so we have gone further in our studies with regard to reconstruction than they have done in the republic to the south of us, and certainly in the old country.
Four or five subcommittees have been formed by the committee, exactly as was done last year by the committee on the rehabilitation of soldiers, and about twenty major studies have been entered upon, some of which are completed, in regard to practically every phase of our economic life and structure in Canada. I would ask my hon. friends, did we not succeed very well last year when we called before the committee on pensions and soldier problems those men who had devoted month after month to the study of these problems. The committee itself had before it the most complete details with reference to every single suggestion tha't had been advanced. In its wisdom the committee made a report to parliament and 90 per cent of the report has been implemented by legislation since that time.
Surely, therefore, the proper procedure at this time is to refer the matter to a committee of this house, and the parliamentary committee can call in those six distinguished gentlemen, men representing every walk of life, who have been so kind as to give their time to the question. On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. HANSON (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
I desire to ask the Minister of National Defence a question on a matter of public importance, and also, I think, on the ground of privilege. During the debate on the United Kingdom financing resolution on Friday last, the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. LaCroix), as reported at page 1494 of Hansard, made reference to a certain report, No. 47, sent out by the military intelligence section of the Department of National Defence, entitled "Summary of Intelligence from Military Districts", and he
1584	COMMONS
Privilege-Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury)
read paragraph 13, which he stated included a report from the intelligence officer of the fortress of Halifax. My questions are:
1.	Has the attention of the minister been called to this portion of the hon. member's speech?
2.	Will the minister advise the house how the hon. member came into possession of what I assume to be a confidential military intelligence release?
3.	What does the minister propose to do about the matter in the premises?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
The hon. member told me that he intended to ask about this matter. May I say categorically that my attention has been called to the report of the speech to which he refers.
Secondly, "with regard to the matter of how it got into the hands of the hon. member I have not the faintest idea. I can only say that whoever gave it to the hon. member gave it without authority and in complete breach of duty, and that a most rigorous investigation is being conducted to ascertain who was responsible for the hon. member obtaining this copy. Further, I want to say that intelligence reports of this class are solely for the secret and confidential information of certain senior officers at National Defence headquarters and of district officers commanding. This particular class of report has, I understand, the most limited circulation of any reports of the Department of National Defence.
I note that the report of the speech refers to it as propaganda. Reports are not propaganda in any sense of the word; they are confidential reports on all sorts of conditions as the officer reporting sees them. Their weight, of course, depends on the capacity of the officer who happens to prepare them. As I have said, the report was given to the hon. member without authority and in breach of duty, but the responsibility for making it public and propaganda devolves entirely on the hon. member who submitted it to this house. As is plainly stated, it is simply a report indicating what the officer considered to be the views of a section-I emphasize that because that is the word used in the report-[DOT] of the active army. In no sense is it intended to represent the views of the army, or of the minister, or of any officer of the department. Intelligence reports deal, as the house will understand, with all sorts of views which affect men's thinking, no matter how unfounded or inaccurate the views may be. All that the report does is indicate that these different viewpoints exist.

I call the attention of hon. members to the fact that no conclusion whatever is drawn, and, contrary to what the hon. member said in his speech, there is not the slightest reflection in the world against French-Canadians who enlist in the army.
The hon. member asks what is proposed to be done about the matter. I have just indicated that the most rigorous investigation is being conducted to find out who was responsible for the hon. member receiving this copy, and appropriate action will be taken according to the circumstances. I also want to say that at some appropriate time when the opportunity arises, I intend to tell the house what has been and is being done in the Department of National Defence to recognize, support and make just as effective as possible the war activities of French-speaking Canadians as far as the army is concerned.

speechtext: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance) moved the third reading of Bill No. 15, for granting to his majesty aid for the purpose of financing United Kingdom war requirements in Canada and for national defence and security.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext:
Before the bill is read the third time, I wish to say briefly that I hope the minister will consider some method of dealing with the securities of Canadian industries and so forth, held in Great Britain. As I said last night, I have given a good deal of thought to this matter and I believe it is of some importance to the country in the post-war period. Last night I suggested that these securities might be considered as collateral to the loan of $700,000,000. It was suggested to me that perhaps to enforce the taking up of these securities from the people who now ov^n them might involve some hardship, and that, instead, an arrangement might be made whereby an understanding could be reached with the British government so that in the event of any of the securities now privately held in Great Britain coming into the market for resale, particularly markets abroad, Canada should have an option on all such securities. That might be less drastic than I proposed yesterday and on previous occasions, but I believe it would, to some degree at least, safeguard this dominion and prevent the
resale of any of these Canadian securities now held by British investors or in Great Britain on, say the New York or some other market, and to that extent our interests would be protected.
I feel, as I said yesterday, that we have made a great gift to Great Britain to the extent of $1,000,000,000, and I do not think anyone would expect this country to make an additional loan of $700,000,000 and forego the opportunity of asking that any Canadian securities now held in Britain, offered for sale, should be first of all offered to the Canadian government so that we may safeguard our interest in that connection.

subtopic: UNITED KINGDOM FINANCING-WAR SUPPLIES, FOOD AND LOAN WITHOUT INTEREST
speechtext: (Translation) Mr. Speaker, before proceeding with the third reading of this bill for the purpose of granting Great Britain a gift of $1,000 million, I wish to record my opposition to the measure. This vast amount represents an average contribution of almost four millions and a quarter for each constituency in Canada. My electors have in no way authorized me to make such a gift. I followed very closely the discussions which have taken place here as well as those in committee. In all earnestness I have been unable to understand just how this financial aid of $1,000,000,000 would be more helpful to Great Britain in the form of a gift than in the form of a loan. Nor have I been able to understand what motive can inspire or explain the zeal manifested by some, a zeal which leads them to exhibit so false a patriotism. However, since this house has already accepted the principle, I suppose this assistance to Britain is as good as granted. Yet there is still time to amend its form. I therefore humbly propose to the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) that this amount be loaned and not given outright to the United Kingdom. I trust that the minister will find this suggestion reasonable and that all members of this house will support it.
Motion agreed to, and bill read the third time and passed.

There was considerable discussion with regard to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, which is amended by this bill, after which the committee reported the bill without amendment. The main point of discussion was the question whether the provision now in the act to the effect that even after the 80-eent restriction on the government is removed, it still applies to the category that runs from eight to twelve bushels to the acre. In order to explain that, I may say that the act now provides that the government cannot declare a year an emergency year if the price of wheat is over 80 cents a bushel. We have removed that restriction; but the act also provides that when wheat is over 70 cents a bushel, so far as the category from eight to twelve bushels to the acre is concerned, for every cent wheat advances beyond 70 cents, 10 cents is taken off the amount paid. The total amount paid in that category is $1, so that when wheat reaches 80 cents that category goes out; and since we have increased the advance from 70 to 90 cents, this automatically puts that category out.
Most of the discussion in the committee was as to whether we should recommend back to the house that the government give consideration to amending that section of the act in order to put that category back in, and the committee decided, by a majority vote, not to make that recommendation. I am not doing that, Mr. Chairman. I am only pointing out that during the course of the discussion of this and the other wheat legislation there has been considerable argument as between distributing farm income on a bushelage basis and distributing farm income on an acreage basis. The argument has been made repeatedly that the fairest way to distribute income is on the acreage basis; and one of the principal reasons advanced for not raising the price of wheat any higher is that it is supposed to be fairer to distribute income on the basis of acreage. I merely want to point out to the committee that those who believed in that point of view are the very people who, by their failure to include that provision in this bill, are preventing large numbers of people from benefiting under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. I think the figures placed on Hansard during the discussion on second reading show that between thirty and thirty-five thousand people each year, of those receiving benefits under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, came within the eight to twelve bushel category. They constituted about 63 per cent of the number receiving bonuses, but now those people will be excluded from the ambit of this legislation.
I think that is unfortunate; I think it argues against all the theories that have been advanced by those who have been claiming in the house for the past two weeks that the fairest way to distribute farm income is on an acreage basis. This legislation is doing just

Wheat Acreage Reduction
the opposite; it is reducing the distribution on an acreage basis and increasing the distribution on a bushelage basis.
When the matter was before the committee some of us moved an amendment that a recommendation be sent back from the committee asking this house to reconsider the bill and to amend the section in order to permit the eight to twelve bushel group to come in. Unfortunately that was voted down. If I remember correctly, the minister intimated that he was not prepared to recommend it to the cabinet in council. I think that is too bad, and much disappointment will be the result.
As has been said repeatedly, this piece of legislation has now become an established measure in dealing with the problem of crop failure in western Canada. It is the basis upon which ultimately it may be possible to build some type of crop insurance scheme. No one suggests that it is crop insurance; but it is a move in that direction, and by widening, extending and modifying the act, it may be possible to base a proper crop insurance scheme on this legislation. A great many people have come to look upon it as something upon which they could depend in those years when, for some cause beyond their control, they have not been able to get adequate crops. Now 63 per cent of those people will be excluded by virtue of the fact that the price of wheat is being established at 90 cents, and the government having failed to bring down an amendement to make the proviso, those people will not be shut out.
I wish merely to make my protest. I do not believe there is any use in labouring the point, or in holding up the bill. If the minister and the government are determined not to bring in the amendment, then all we can do is to do what we did in committee, namely ask the government to take the matter into consideration, with a view to bringing down an amendment next year. That would seem to be the proper procedure, if the government is not prepared to take action now. Just as to-day the price is fixed at 70 cents, and every time the price of wheat rises above 70 cents, the bonus of the 8- to 12-bushel group is reduced 10 cents an acre, it would have been equally fair to raise the price to 90 cents and to have said that every time the price of wheat rises one cent above 90 cents the bonus should be reduced 10 cents an acre. It seems to me that would have been fair and equitable as between tlhe different groups suffering crop failure. If the government is not prepared to take this step now, I hope it will at least take the matter into consideration with a view to doing so at a later date.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext:
I do not like this section as it stands. I might point out that the agriculture committee did not like it either, and they moved that the section should be struck out and another substituted. Another section was drafted, and the Minister of Agriculture himself spoke in favour of the other section which was drawn up. He also pointed out that, since the new section would mean an increase in expenditures, it would have to be referred to the cabinet. This was done, and they refused to accept it.
There are many reasons why this section as it stands before us now is undesirable. In the first place, the government asked the farmers of western Canada to cooperate in 1940 by reducing their acreage. A very large number of farmers did cooperate and now, as a result of that cooperation, they are being penalized under this section. Section 3 reads:
For the purposes of this act, the basic acreage in wheat on any farm in the area shall be the wheat acreage in 1940. . . .
Last year under the regulations we stated that the basic acreage would be dependent upon the 1939 and 1940 acreage; in other words, we said that if the average of 1939-40 wheat acreage was less than 60 per cent of the total cultivated acreage we would take the higher of the two. If we take the bill as it stands, the farmer's basic acreage is

Wheat Acreage Reduction
dependent upon the 1940 acreage alone and there will be a considerably smaller amount paid to the farmers.
The minister said that the definition we had last year had caused a great deal of delay in making the payment; that looking back over the 1939 records had occasioned a good deal of trouble, for the reason that many of the farmers had not kept records, and he blamed that largely for the delay. The point is, however, that we have now done all that work and that basic acreage has been established so that there can not be any delay this year from that cause. If we are now going to take the new basic acreage, it means that all the work we did last year will have been done for nothing. The suggestion the committee made was that, for the farmers who applied under the act last year, the basic acreage as established last year would be used, and for the farmers who did not make application last year, the new basic acreage would be used.
I would say to the government that as soon as it becomes known that we are taking the 1940 acreage as the basic acreage, there will be discontent throughout the west. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) will be flooded with protests. Imagine what is being done! Many farmers in 1940 had only about twenty or thirty acres of wheat out of a total of 400 acres of cultivated land, and now the government is saying that that twenty or thirty acres shall constitute the basic acreage, although the total cultivated acreage may be 400 acres. Can any minister justify that? There is absolutely no justice in this section. Last year we discussed this whole question fully in the house for days and finally came to the conclusion that the only fair way to deal with the matter was to take the average of 1939 and 1940 and, where that average was less than 60 per cent, to take the higher. Even now at this late hour the government should reconsider their action. The Minister of Agriculture himself had endorsed the alternative section.
While we are on this section I might be allowed to say, so far as this measure is concerned, that we would have been better off if we had given the farmers $1 a bushel and increased the price, as we are doing, for oats, barley and flax. The farmers, under the present proposal, will not be satisfied. A dollar a bushel plus a sound crop insurance plan would have given satisfaction, and we could have eliminated this measure; but seeing that we are keeping it in operation I submit that we should do everything in our power to put it on an equitable basis.
The minister himself knows that section 3 is not equitable, and it will cause a great deal of discontent in the west. I do not think a single member of the house heard any criticism from any farmer in regard to section 3 as it read last year. We spent a great deal of time in working it out and it was fair, but in order to save a few dollars the cabinet is now prepared to sacrifice the old section and put in this one, which is decidedly unjust.

With regard to this particular section I voted for the clause as it now stands in the bill and as it was in the bill when brought before the committee. As a matter of fact, I presented the bill to the house and recommended that the house accept it, and I also did the same so far as the committee was concerned.
When the matter was under discussion in the committee two proposals were made. One was that we accept the acreage of 1940 as the basis from which the reduction would be made this year-that is, the actual acreage of 1940. That is the provision which is made in the bill. The other was that we accept the assumed acreage for 1940, which was provided by taking the average between 1939 and 1940. The discussion began with that, and I pointed out to the committee that the reason for putting this proposal in the bill was the great amount of criticism which came from all over western Canada during 1941 because of the delays in making payment, which delays were almost without exception due to the fact that we had the average of 1939 and 1940. That is to say, if we had simply taken the 1940 acreage and had it sworn to, that would have been a sworn statement of one year's crop and we would have had to consider only that one year. As it was, however, we asked the farmer to go back to 1939 and give his acreage for that year; and when he did so, in many cases, he made mistakes of 5 or 10 acres on the total crop acreage and, in some instances, 20 or 30 acres. Immediately the mistake was re-
Wheat Acreage Reduction

ported to the treasury, the treasury officials refused to pay the amount claimed until the reason for the mistake was established or until the figures were corrected.
Most of the criticism that came in during the summer was caused by the attempt to average. I did make the suggestion, as an alternative to the proposal made by certain members of the committee, that we might get over some of the difficulty which I had in mind if we were to make the 1940 average apply to the new applicants and leave the provisions, with regard to those who had been paid last year, as they were in the regulations of last year. I suggested that I would take that to council and have it discussed, and if council were satisfied to provide the additional expenditure made necessary by that provision, then the matter could be brought back to the committee and agreed to. I took it to council, but council did not agree to have the additional expenditure made. The section as it was in the bill when referred to the committee, has been brought back to the house.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: In my opinion the recommendation of the committee should have been considered. As was pointed out in the committee, considerable work was done last year, and that work is now going to be lost in the coming year. More than that, those farmers who did not cooperate last year will be brought in under a different basis from that on which the others will stand. The committee were fairly unanimous that the recommendation should have been carried out in an amendment to section 3. Surely those people who did not cooperate last year Should not be brought in now on a basis different from that on which the vast number stand, who really played ball last year. I suggest that the administration will have a good deal of extra work to do, and administration of the measure will cost more money. I regret that the minister has not seen fit to get the cabinet to agree to amend the section.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext:
The members of the committee will recall that last year just before the Easter recess the minister brought down his regulations regarding wheat acreage reduction. Most of the western members took copies of the regulations west with them during the Easter recess to endeavour to explain them to their constituents. I think the experience of the minister was probably the same as that of other hon. members, that in almost every public meeting farmers came and pointed out with some indignation that they had acquiesced in the request to reduce wheat acreage, and they said "Now you are going to penalize those of us who acquiesced, and pay the man who did not follow the min-
(Mr. Gardiner.]
ister's suggestion." When we assembled after Easter most of the western members made representations to the minister asking if it were not possible to remove what looked like discrimination. The minister agreed and a new basis was worked out. I agree with the minister that probably it did mean a good deal of extra work and did produce administrative difficulties, and I would be the last to ask the minister to go through that again, trying to harmonize the wheat acreage of the two years. But that has now been established for all the farmers who came into this scheme.
This arrangement is going to be veiy confusing for these people. A certain wheat acreage has been established; this year when they apply for the bonus they are going to find that they are being paid on a totally different basis. They will be coming to members of parliament; they will be going to the offices in Regina or to see the supervisors, and we shall have the same thing we had last fall all over again. I am sorry for the minister's own sake and the sake of those who have to administer the legislation if it is not possible merely to send out notification to each of the farmers who came under this legislation last year saying, "Your basic wheat acreage is so much; that is established. The basis on which you were paid last year is the basis on which you will be paid this year. On any reduction below that figure you will be paid S2 an acre." But under this section the 'basis is changed, we shall have to go through it again for readjustment, which will make the legislation more difficult to administer.

speechtext: I wonder whether the minister would explain further why certain officials should be given these cheques to deliver to people personally. To me this seems a very improper procedure for any government department to allow.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: If the facts are as they were stated by the lawyer who wrote in, then it would be an improper practice, and we would, of course, require to discipline the official. We are checking up on the case, as a matter of fact; and if we find the facts are as they have been stated to be, then we shall have to take action which will bear proper relation to any wrong that may have been committed. But until we are certain of that, I should not like to discuss the matter further than we have.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: Has the man been suspended in the meantime?

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: No; sufficient grounds have not, up to the moment, been established upon which to order suspension.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: How did the cheques get into the hands of this individual, when the ordinary system is that they are sent out directly by the treasury department to the recipient? How did this individual get hold of the cheques and place himself in a position where, by intimidation, he could influence these people to endorse the cheques to him?

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: I think there is too much being inferred in the remarks being made. I do not know that there was any intimidation, or that the cheques were got in any way other than what might be considered a proper way. That is, if an individual wrote to me, and I was going home to that particular place, he might ask me to bring the cheque along with me. In other words, he would ask me to be the carrier of his mail, so to speak, and I might not object to doing it. If those are the circumstances, then I do not think anyone would consider there had been much of an offence committed. We are going into that part of it now, just to find out what the basis of the complaint is.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: Why did the treasury branch hand the cheques out in that way?

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: In this particular case in hand, the persons concerned were all at the man's own home.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext:
He took the cheques home, and then made a call.

Wheat Acreage Reduction

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: That answer is scarcely satisfactory. It still does not answer my question as to how it came about that this cheque got into this individual's hands, when he is an official in the department. How did he get these cheques? It is all very well to suggest that he may have carried the mail. Does the minister say there is even a suggestion that he ever carried the mail?

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: This particular man's mail; he may have been asked to take it; I do not know.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: How would this man, carrying the mail, get possession of cheques sent out by the treasury department- or which should be sent out by the treasury department?

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: It is a very simple matter to write a letter to the treasury, when the two offices are operating in the same building. It is a very simple matter for that to happen in a case of that kind. I think, however, all of the facts will be made known in due course.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: How many instances were there?

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: I am not in a position to say, because it has not yet been investigated fully.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: Whether it has been investigated or not, how many complaints have been made?

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: Covering how many individuals?

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: Covering, as far as I [DOT]emember, three individuals. The complaint is based, I think, on three affidavits.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: And against one official?

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: Yes, one official.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: Is that official still carrying on, while the investigation is proceeding?

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: He is still carrying on, until he has an opportunity to make an explanation.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: And still carrying the cheques?

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext:
Do we understand the minister to say, with respect to the payment of this money, that no creditor can collect the 
money from a farmer? Does this mean that it is set aside, and that it cannot be collected by any creditor?

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: It cannot be attached while it is in the possession of the government. But after the cheque is issued, anyone could collect, of course, if he can find a way of doing so.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: And if it has not been spent.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: So long as he summer-fallows in excess of what he summer-fallowed last year, can he summer-fallow his whole farm?

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: Yes, he could summer-fallow his whole farm.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: And if he were insolvent, it would pay him to keep on summer-fallowing, would it not?

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: No, not very well. It would not pay him to keep on summerfallowing at $2 an acre if he can grow twenty bushels to the acre, to sell at 90 cents.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: With respect to section 5, I would point out that a year ago the minister's department advertised widely the regulations brought out. An important change has been made in connection with the basic period. What arrangements have been made this year to publicize the changes which have been introduced? Last year a number of people were unable to take advantage of the regulations because of not filing their applications in time. I can anticipate that because of confusion over changes there might be some difficulty this year. What plans have been made?

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext:
The question is as to what arrangements have been made to make the farmer acquainted with the changes in the legislation this year compared with that of last year. My answer is that advertisements are in the west to be placed in the hands of the local press in western Canada, and those advertisements are to appear immediately the bill passes this house. The advertisements give the farmers full information as to this year's policy. Then, announcements will be made over the radio, and addresses will be given to audiences throughout western Canada by officials of the provincial and federal departments. The information with regard to the whole matter will be in the hands of every municipal secretary in the three western provinces, as it was last year. I know of no reason why farmers should not be made acquainted with any changes made.

Wheat Acreage Reduction

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: The minister will recall that last year many orders in council were passed after July. I have at least three of them in mind1. The definition of "summer-fallow" was changed on November 27. While I am prepared to accept and support the bill, I think the minister should make it clear that a number of orders in council will not be passed in mid-summer changing any of the sections of the bill. He should make it clear to the farmers that this is final, and that there will no changes such as the one with respect to the definition of "summer-fallow", to which I have referred. Last year it was most confusing to have orders in council come out a month or so after the summer-fallowing had been completed.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: It would seem that the farmer is paid $2 for those areas sown to grass. What happens if the grass does not grow? Does he still get the $2 because it was sown to grass?
