speechtext: If he takes it out of wheat this year and seeds it to grass-

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: And the grass does not grow.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: Well, we need not deal with that alone for the time being. Anything else may not grow, either.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: But you pay him. anyway?

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext:
If he seeds it to coarse
grain, grass or rye, he receives $2 an acre.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: On the theory that it is wheat reduction?

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: Yes. Even if he summer-fallows it and does not put in anything, he still gets the $2 because he is taking it out of wheat. In addition if he does sow, and grows a crop the succeeding year, he gets an additional $2 in that year.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext:
He gets $2 for not sowing
wheat and $2 for sowing grass.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: I listened with a good deal of interest to the criticism made by the hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Homuth) in connection with these cheques. I do not know enough about the subject to express a definite opinion, but I would ask the minister this question: A tenant farmer farming land he does not own, and possessing no assets, engages a man to work for him. That man works for the farmer for some time and is not paid any wages. A cheque is coming to the tenant farmer. Has that workman any redress? Is there any way in which he can get his money? I ask this question because on one occasion I worked very hard for a threshing outfit in the west and never got my money.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: That dispute would be settled now under the landlords and tenants act, or masters and servants act, which is provincial legislation, and not under any legislation passed here.

Section agreed to.
Sections 5 to 9 inclusive agreed to.
On section 10-Regulations.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: Is it the understanding of the minister that the regulations contemplated by section 10 are limited to the question of enforcement and administration of the measure and are in no sense to be made an extension of the principle of the measure as was the case under the summer-fallow provisions of last year? In other words these regulations are strictly limited to the enforcement and administration of the legislation and cannot go beyond that. Is that his understanding?

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: This bill as now drafted is practically 100 per cent the regulations of last year.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext:
I understand that.
Wheat Acreage Reduction

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext:
Last year the whole policy was put into effect by regulations. This year the only power we have with regard to regulations is the power given in this particular section, which provides:
The minister may, with the approval of the governor in council, make such regulations as may be deemed necessary for the efficient enforcement and administration of this act.
We shall not be able to change the principle *of the bill by any regulations.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: That is what I was calling attention to. It is a very limited1 power of regulation.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am
pleased indeed to congratulate the government upon its announcement this afternoon exempting the farmers from military training and I should like, through the Minister of Agriculture, to thank the government for its action on this very important national question.

Section agreed to.
On section 11-Offences and penalties.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: I draw the attention of the committee to the amendments as read by the minister. In line 24 "wilfully" is inserted before "submits" and in line 25 "knowingly" is inserted before "makes". In line 28 "wilfully" is added after "who" and in line 29 "knowingly" is inserted before "makes."

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: Has the minister taken the opinion of his legal advisers on the effect of the insertion of the words "wilfully" and "knowingly" in these two paragraphs? I suggest to the minister that if he insists on the inclusion of these two words, he will probably never be able to get a conviction.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I should like the hon. gentleman to elaborate that a little. It would be a very serious consequence, if so.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: It is no reflection on anybody. I am not going to go into an elaborate discussion here of the theory of intent, but I know how difficult it is to prove it apart from the mere submission of a document. I am not going to object at all. I think it is a protection to the treasury. I simply point out that in the administration of justice, if you insert these words, it is going to be just that more difficult to get a conviction.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext:
I certainly did not intend to say anything on this bill, but the treasury officials who institute these prosecutions consider it of the utmost importance that they

be able to get convictions in cases of true fraud, of which there have been some. I wish to make it perfectly clear that my understanding of the amendments to this section is that they do not change the section one bit.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: It makes it more difficult to prove the offence, that is all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: I would not have agreed to this amendment if I had thought it would enable persons to get away with fraudulent claims. I do not believe it does. I do not believe that a conviction should be secured for submitting false information unless it was knowingly submitted, and I would be surprised if any conviction was ever obtained in cases where an innocent mistake was made in giving information. I certainly hope that we have not ruined this section by putting in these words, because there will be the odd case of fraudulent claim, and it is of extreme importance, of importance I would think to everybody interested in the measure, that the fraudulent claimant be punished. The honest claimants, who are in the overwhelming majority, would themselves want the fraudulent claimant punished for the reputation of the community and of the legislation. I would not like the legal advice of the leader of the opposition to go out to a certain class of individuals, to the effect that they can now get .away with anything because the words "knowingly" and "wilfully" are in the legislation.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: The minister is imputing something I never suggested. I simply tell him as a practising lawyer that the inclusion of "wilfully" and "knowingly" in this clause is going to make it very difficult to get a conviction, and I am in the judgment of every practising lawyer in this house when I make that statement.

Section agreed to.
Section 12 agreed to.
On section 13-Officers and employees.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: Does the minister think it will require as large a staff to administer this *bill as he had last smar? Last year everything was done by regulation under order in council. The principle of those regulations and orders in council are embodied in this bill. A lot of inspection has been done in the last year or two, and does the minister not think that the staff can now be reduced and a considerable saving effected this coming season in administering this bill as now drafted?

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext:
There is no permanent staff in connection with the administration

Wheat Acreage Reduction
either of this legislation or of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, excepting the staff in the offices, and a very few superintendents of districts covering the three prairie provinces. The other persons employed, that is the inspectors, are employed only for the time they are required. Some of them have employment for a few weeks, and some for as much as three or four months. I doubt if many have employment for any longer. Of course, those staffs are pretty well reduced at present. It depends entirely upon what we are required to do next summer as to how many men will be called back to work during the summer months. We have followed the practice of calling back those who have given the best service during the years preceding, and we have not called up new men unless we require men for additional work. The number that are on at present is very small. I have the figures here, and could look them up, but it would take some little time to go through the papers I have in front of me.
As we come into the summer months, and applications are made by the 31st of May. we shall be required to make certain inspections, and those inspections will be made. After the 1st of July, when inspections are made for payment and we pass them on to the treasury, there will be cases referred back to us and we may have to engage an additional number of men. The number we shall require will depend largely upon the number of mistakes that are made by farmers when they make their applications. I do not suppose anyone in the house would ask us to have the payments made, where mistakes have occurred, until those errors have been corrected. The more mistakes that are made, the more corrections will be necessary, and the more men will have to be sent out to make inspections. Therefore at the moment I am not in a position to say to what extent we can limit the number of men to be employed, but we will certainly restrict them to the lowest possible number to get the work done. Our costs, in spite of what has been said, have not been high. It has been asserted from time to time that there have been hundreds of inspectors out, one inspector inspecting the other, and so on. But our costs are low, as costs of this type are considered from place to place throughout Canada.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: Were not a considerable number of mistakes made by the inspectors themselves in checking up on this work?

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext:
Of course, all persons are human, and one inspector may think that
a piece of land is not properly summer-fallowed while another man might say that it is. There may be a difference of opinion, and where there is, we usually have to send someone else to arbitrate as between those who differ. All these things cost money and take time.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: How many employees were there last year, and what was the total amount disbursed in the administration of this measure?

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: I had that information before the committee the other day. I am not sure that I have it here; I will see.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: The minister said just now that the cost of administration was fairly low.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: About 4 per cent.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: I should like to point out that the cost of administration for this last year up to February 27, according to sessional paper 153A, was $785,800.42, and the cost of administration under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act-because the inspectors, I understand, are used interchangeably-for last year, also up to February 27, 1942, was 8387,422.07, making a total, roughly, of something over $1,000,000. The amount expended! under the wheat acreage reduction plan to* the same date was, roughly, $26,500,000, and the amount spent in the same period under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act was about $5,326,000. In other words, about $30,000,000 was paid out under these two bonuses, with an administration cost of a little over $1,000,000. I would hardly call that very low.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext:
I have the summary of the staff as at February 28. I am sorry 1 have not before me full information for the entire year.
The staff for the three provinces consists of: one director; one assistant director; three superintendents-one for each province-one accountant; five supervisors in the office; nine inspectors working from the office; two clerks,, grade IV; four clerks, grade III; thirty-two clerks and stenographers, grade II; twenty-eight clerks and stenographers, Grade IA; six clerks and stenographers, grade I; 532 clerks* and stenographers, day basis, for the three provinces, taken on at different times; field staff: thirty-four supervisors, permanent employees, for the three provinces; seventy-four inspectors, making a total of one hundred and eight; or a grand total of 732 in the office and outside.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext:
Is that the number who are engaged at present, or the number hired during the whole year?
Wheat Acreage Reduction

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: That is the number at the date of this return, which was February 28. The number of inspectors would be lower then than during the summer months. There would be more inspectors in the field in the summer; I believe the total number was somewhere between two and three hundred, but I have not the exact figures.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: On what basis are these inspectors and supervisors paid?

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: The supervisors are paid on a monthly basis. I think the highest amount is $150 a month, or $1,800 a year. I should not like to speak from memory with regard to the others. The stenographers, also the clerks, are paid the regular rates which are paid in the civil service. The director, the assistant director and the superintendents are paid on the same basis as persons doing similar work elsewhere in the civil service.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: Would it not be possible to reduce this staff very considerably? According to the information furnished by the hon. member for Weyburn, here is an expenditure of about 3i per cent from the administration of these two acts. There are seventy-four inspectors in the winter time looking after summer-fallow, or wheat acreage reduction.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: Well, now, that is not a fair statement. My hon. friend knows that.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: What is the purpose of having those inspectors in the winter time? WThy have them all the year round?

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: To keep the snow off the summer-fallow!

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: The hon. member for Lake Centre only needs to look at this own. files, and so does every other member from western Canada, to get the answer to that. maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: Because of delays.

speechtext:

That requires, of course, that any mistakes which are made be corrected. In the winter time we are checking many of these claims which have been made. We check with the operators of the elevators, the secretaries of municipalities and any other indi-
IMr. T. C. Douglas.]
vidual who may know anything at all about the business transactions of a man who is making a claim, and attempt during that period to establish his claim so that it oan be paid.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: In this respect I understand that no matter how correct a claim which is filed may be, or how favourable the report made by the ordinary field inspector, any item of over $1,000 is not paid until a second inspection is made. maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: I would not wish to answer that question by saying they are made one way or the other in all instances. In some instances a second or third inspection may be made by the treasury. I believe that in all instances the second inspection has been made by the Department of Agriculture.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: That is for payments over $1,000.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: The minister has not given me all the information I want. There have been many criticisms in my constituency about these inspectors doing too much travelling. I do not know whether it is well founded, but the complaint is made that they drive back and forth morning and night in order to build up mileage. maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: Is that more than they actually pay in hotels?

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext:
I do not think so; it is not supposed to be. It will cover hotel bills -meals as well as lodging.

Wheat Acreage Reduction

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ACREAGE REDUCTION AND CERTAIN PAYMENTS TO FARMERS
speechtext: How much per day?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the resolution now under discussion is advanced a stage, I should like U make a few brief remarks in connection with our war effort. First of all, I should like to
War Appropriation

associate myself with the remarks made last night by tihe hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) who expressed the hope that the few remaining days before tlhe Easter adjournment would be devoted entirely to a discussion of our war effort. In my opinion it is most unfortunate that during this session, which is now in its third month, we should have spent so much time in the discussion of the speech from the throne, the plebiscite, the question of wheat and so on, while practically no time at all has been available for the discussion of Canada's war effort.
Naturally all hon. members were greatly interested in the statement made this afternoon by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), but it is unfortunate that it is nearly two years since the registration was taken, and only now is the government making any attempt to put into force a comprehensive and extensive man-power scheme. Every hon. member knows of many cases in his own riding in which available man-power is being wasted. In my riding, which is largely agricultural, I find that even to-day cheese-makers are being called up for military training. I submit that a qualified eheesemaker is a highly skilled man in connection with our war effort. During the past few weeks meetings have been held in many agricultural ridings in Ontario, under the auspices of the provincial agricultural representatives, at which they have given cheese and bacon producers pep talks, pointing out to them the urgent need of increasing the production of bacon, cheese, cream, butter and all other foodstuffs. I do not think it is necessary to give pep talks to the farmers of Ontario in order to get them to produce more, because they are only too anxious to bring about maximum production. They ask for only two things-a fair price and that they be given some assistance in the matter of farm help. The remarks of the Prime Minister to-day in regard to farm help will receive most careful examination.
I had intended to say something at this time about the situation in connection with appeals by farmers to district boards, but I shall reserve that for a later date, after I have studied the statement given to-day. The Prime Minister stated that there would be further appeals, and that probably the boards would have to be greatly extended. I do not know under what department it comes, but I should like to point out that at the present time the military district in which Ottawa is located, being military district No. 3, includes an area extending practically from the town of Boman-ville well into the province of Quebec. In this area are many centres of population, such as Peterborough, Lindsay, Belleville, Kingston, 
Ottawa and part of Quebec. The headquarters of this board is located in the city of Kingston, and appeals to the board may be made in person or by letter.
The point I should like to stress is that in future, when there will be many more appeals heard, would it not be better to have these boards visit the various counities in each military district two, three or four times a year, sitting at three or four of the* main towns in each county. Then all appeals could be heard in person. At the present time representations are made by letter, and I submit that it is only proper and fair and just that all appeals should be heard in person, and in person only. If some such system as this were worked out, it would remove much of the rising criticism which we hear at the present time.
I wish to say a few words about the number of men in our reserve forces. Under the last book issued by the Minister of National War Services (Mr. Thorson), I believe he listed them somewhere between
140.000	and 150,000 men. My understanding is that the men in the reserve forces are made up of three classes: First, the men who were called for thirty days' training, numbering some 87,000 or 89,000, who took thirty days' training and then returned to their homes. I believe, according to the minister's statement, some 20,000 of those men have since enlisted in the active forces.
The second class of men in the reserve army are the men who were called for four months' training and retained in the army, and the men who have been called since the four months' training scheme was dropped. How many of these men have been called, I do not know, but I believe some 10,000 or
15.000	of them have enlisted in the active forces. The other men who make up the reserve army are the second battalions, and various other units who take their training at their local headquarters. The men who were called for thirty days' training have not yet received any further training-except the men who have been called back for further training.
I submit that the total number of men in our reserve army to-day is only the total number of men who have been called up for the duration of the war and who, so far as I can figure, amount to something like 50,000 men, or thereabouts. That is a great deal short of the 140,000 or 150,000 shown by the minister in his little blue booklet.
A short time ago an order was issued whereby some of these reserve force units would be brigaded. I believe the brigade for military district No. 3 is in the city of Ottawa. But there are many other reserve

War Appropriation
force units in this district which are still orphans. I think the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) must surely realize at this late date that he cannot hope to train men in the reserve army by training two nights a week for two or three hours, with obsolete equipment.
The type of training carried on by these reserve force units consists in many instances of simply parade ground drill, and elementary rifle and bayonet practice. In many instances this is the only type of drill they can take, because they have no other equipment. I have read in the press at various times that the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) has stated that he can equip a division every six weeks. If this means that he can fully equip a division every six weeks, what, then, is the reason why reserve force units have so little and, in many instances, no equipment for training purposes? These men in the reserve forces cannot continue to be trained in the Boer war methods any longer, because very soon these men may be called upon to engage in fighting an enemy who is fully equipped, highly trained and fully mechanized in the 1942 method of conducting a war.
When are those men in the reserve force units going to receive advance training, or when will they receive instructions on mortars, Tommy guns, grenades, or take part in manoeuvres or advanced military tactics in connection with planes, Bren gun carriers, tanks and so on?
If an emergency arose and these reserve force men were called out to engage an enemy, I submit that it would be only criminal to expect them to fight and to engage an enemy equipped with, modern weapons. I have on various other occasions in the house attempted to impress upon the Minister of National Defence the importance of time. Time is the one great factor in this war. I should like to ask the minister why these reserve force units cannot be called up and placed on fulltime training. There are dozens of armouries across this dominion which are used to no purpose, except for reserve force units. Any member of the house who has visited a modern training centre must have been impressed by the manner in which these training centres are equipped, and also impressed with the very highly skilled and trained officers and non-commissioned officers, and men on the permanent staff. Trained personnel of the army is a very, very important factor to-day.
I would suggest to the minister that in order to increase the number of men now being trained, dozens of armouries throughout Canada should be used for basic training. At
the present time the basic training is taken at various training centres. If the men could receive their training-

I am sure there are plenty of officers in the reserve force and plenty of non-commissioned officers in that force, also many veterans of the last war who are quite capable of carrying on and conducting basic training at local armouries. If some such system were adopted, the number of recruits passing through training centres could be practically doubled every two months. If this were done, the reserve force units would then be performing some useful purpose. As they are constituted at the present time, and as they train at present they are practically useless; and the cost of maintaining these dozens of armouries with partial staffs and small administrative and training staffs, and all the other thousand and one items which enter into military expenditures, must be enormous. Each year very large sums are spent on the reserve force units, and in my opinion the results do not justify these huge expenditures.
There is the further point, that if we are to continue the voluntary system of enlistment in Canada-and apparently that is the only system we are going to have-the reserve force units could do a great deal in supplying recruits for the active forces.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) has just placed before the house a bill providing for a gift of a billion dollars to Great Britain. There are in his name on the order paper other bills totalling over two billion dollars. Certainly these are staggering sums. Apparently he deals only in millions and billions. But when he comes to dealing with the soldiers he gets down to pinching pennies, for the first time. In the last session members from all parts of the house urged the government to consider a revision of rates of pay and allowances for boys in the armed forces. True, there was some slight adjustment in
War Appropriation

regard to the third and fourth child; but that was really nothing very much, because it should have been that way since the war started in 1939.

speechtext:
Everyone admits that the cost of living has greatly increased since September, 1939. The government has recognized this by granting a cost of living bonus; but, strange to say, it does not apply to the armed forces. How strange that everyone else in this Canada of ours who is doing any kind of war work receives the highest of wages; yet the men in the armed forces, the only men in Canada who are really making any sacrifice, are discriminated against because they receive no increase in pay, no increase in living allowance, and their dependents are forced to get along on the scale established in September, 1939. I submit to the minister that there is nothing political whatever about this request for an increase in pay for the soldiers, since members of all parties have urged the government to give consideration to making some such adjustment. I sincerely trust that in the very near future the minister will announce that even at this late date something will be done in the matter of adjusting the soldier's pay, and I can assure him that it would have some effect on recruiting, because undoubtedly a young man to-day can earn a great deal more money and enjoy a great many more privileges and comforts by undertaking war work in a factory than by joining the army.
I noticed on the bulletin board of a local newspaper this morning that there were three air attacks on England last night, the first for months, the warming-up for the spring offensive that is soon to break. It will break within a matter of days on all fronts round the world. Here in Canada what are we doing about a spring offensive?

speechtext:
Our spring offensive in our appeasement policy will open on the 27th day of April when the people of Canada will be asked to vote "yes" or "no" on a meaningless question. What a fine contribution to our allies of the united nations! Only a few days ago in this house the members 
heard the Prime Minister read a statement that had been issued by Anthony Eden disclosing the atrocities and vengeance wreaked by Japanese soldiers on helpless Canadian and British war prisoners at Hong Kong. Members heard how a ruthless, barbarian, savage yellow enemy raped and ravished white women and girls.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: How could any member sit in this house and hear that report read without his very soul being filled with rage and vows of vengeance upon this enemy? Yet, when the Prime Minister had finished his statement, we calmly proceeded with our plebiscite proceedings. I fully expected that after the Prime Minister had made that statement he would have announced that the plebiscite had gone by the board and that we would at last get on with a total war effort. In my riding there are many boys who enlisted and1 went to Hong Kong.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: My patience is almost exhausted. The hon. member is deliberately defying the Chair. I cannot allow that to continue, and I warn the hon. gentleman now that if he persists in further interruptions, I shall certainly name him. I hope he will not put that unpleasant duty upon me.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
There are many boys in my riding who went to Hong Kong, and it would not be well for anybody to go into that riding and ask the parents, brothers, sisters, wives and sweethearts of any of those boys, what they think about the plebiscite or whether they think that Canada should at this late date make a total war effort, nor would it be wise for anybody to go into my riding, which, of all the ridings in Canada, has probably the largest percentage of men in the armed forces, and ask the parents and families of those boys who have gone overseas what they think about the plebiscite and whether they think we should wage total war at this late date.
This yellow peril is coming closer and closer to our shores every day. If Australia falls, what happened at Hong Kong and Singapore will happen here. The very thought of such outrages happening in this country should be enough to make us finish with our appeasement ways and decide at once to make a total war effort and wage total war, which our enemies have done from the day war started. Surely our days of complacency and appeasement should end now, because what happened in Hong Kong and Singapore can happen here

War Appropriation
and probably will happen here. In the few remaining days that are left to us before the storm breaks, are we bending every effort and making every preparation we can? Are we mobilizing all our resources and making plans for every possible emergency, or are we still living in a fairyland and saying that it cannot happen here? I believe it is a time-honoured custom of the British parliament that before supply is granted, members shall receive all possible information.
There is another reason why we should receive information at this time. We are sometimes accused of not cooperating with the government and of retarding the work of the administration. I submit that it is becoming more and more difficult to get any reliable information from this government. If we want to know what the government is doing, we have to go either to the press room or to the Financial Post.
I will give the house a glaring example of the condition of which I complain. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that such treatment of the members of this house is.not good enough, and it is happening every day. It was only yesterday that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) said in reference to certain subsidies which are to be paid in conne.ction with the importation of certain food products that he did not know whether he would tell the house who received those subsidies. I should like very much to assist the government, because I am intensely interested in furthering the country's war effort; but I certainly feel that I should be treated as a responsible member of this house. There are a number of other things to which I was going to refer while on my feet, but I do not wish at this stage to mix too many subjects. Having listened to a number of speeches during that long debate, I have been forced to the conclusion that many members of this house have not even yet awakened to the full realization of the news that comes to us daily from all parts of the world. They seem still to believe that the horrors of war cannot touch us. I can best answer them by quoting some significant words of Sir Stafford Cripps: This war is not a game to be played according to certain rules; it is a life and death struggle for survival, and in that struggle there are and must be no partial interests. It is impossible to have regard to the interests of groups and classes and people still keeping in mind what their position is likely to be after the war. and at the same time to make our effort all-inclusive.
Yet we are dawdling along in this house as if we had all eternity before us, and in a few days we shall adjourn for three months' vacation-

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the 40-minute rule with regard to speeches be changed to 15 minutes, which would require that the speeches be more carefully prepared and condensed. In order to illustrate my point I should like to tell a story of a clergyman who was asked if he would give a 15-minute address on a particular occasion. He declined on the ground that he had not time to prepare it. When surprise and disappointment were expressed he said, "I should be glad to give you an address of 40 minutes, because I could speak discursively, but if I have to concentrate and crystallize my remarks into a 15-minute speech I have not time to prepare it." That, I think, is a very apt illustration of a good deal of what we have heard here.
I make the further suggestion, that for the duration of the war Hansard be abolished. This would have the effect of saving a good deal of time and money which could then be devoted to war purposes. We are facing the greatest crisis in our history; the issue soon to be settled is whether we are to be free or slaves. We are up against the greatest combination of superbly trained and magnificently equipped military forces that this world has ever seen, who continue to inflict upon us defeat after defeat. Let us not deceive ourselves, but admit the fact that up to the present we have lost every battle, and unless we make a total war effort by utilizing at once all our resources both physical and human, we shall lose the war in this year 1942.
When Sir Stafford Cripps, who should1 be better informed on the situation in Europe, than any other man, arrived in New Delhi yesterday he said, "There is no time to lose and no time for long discussions." The able representatives of the newspapers in Canada in the press gallery can be relied upon to sift the wheat from the chaff, and I am sure the reading public will not suffer as a consequence of what I propose.
The Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe), speaking on the radio last night, revealed an alarming shortage of rubber, stating that when our present supply is exhausted there will be no more rubber available until the synthetic plants are built and able to produce, rubber. This, I understand, will take from one to two years. So it is quite obvious that our prospect of getting rubber in the near future is very remote. I wonder whether the government have done all that is possible to conserve our rubber supply. Have they taken an inventory of the tires in the hands of manufacturers and dealers throughout the country? Only two weeks ago I was told by a responsible citizen that 
lie had been offered new tires for his car by a dealer who said that up to that time no inventory had been taken of his stock and therefore no one was in a position to check up as to what he did with his tires.
To be caught at this time with a shortage of rubber seems to indicate a lack of foresight on the part of those responsible for our war effort. I was told more than a year ago by a high official in the rubber industry in Canada that Japan was very likely to destroy our major sources of rubber. This man had1 this information; so surely some one connected with the Department of Munitions and Supply or with the war departments of the government would equally have had the opportunity of knowing what the situation was likely to be. Again "too little and too late".
The minister also announced last night that the speed limit wrould be reduced to forty miles an hour. Why not to thirty-five miles an hour? I know that investigators in the laboratories of some of the oil companies have proved that the most economical speed in regard to the use of gasoline and oil is thirty-five miles an hour, which was the speed limit in Ontario until a few years ago. I suggest that it be again reduced to thirty-five miles an hour to save gasoline and rubber tires.
I wish to express my approval of the suggestion made by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) last evening that we send a token force to Australia. We fought side by side in the last war, and I think all hon. members will appreciate what a wonderfully stimulating and encouraging effect that would have upon our brothers down under. The force need not be large, a regiment or a brigade. It would1 be very much better for us to fight Japan in Australia 'than in Vancouver.
I feel that some comment should be made on the recent adoption by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) of the suggestion made by the hon. member for Vancouver South when the minister announced the appointment of officers to the supreme command on the west and east coasts of Canada. We are fighting Germany and Japan whose policy has been and is to require their senior officers to be trained in the three arms of the service-the navy, the air force and the army-before they are given a unified command. May I ask the Minister of National Defence what training the recently appointed commanders in chief on the Pacific and Atlantic coasts have had in the air force and the navy? We have had many indications that our enemies have adopted entirely new methods of warfare, which have been very successful, and if we are to have a chance of

War Appropriation
defeating them we also must adopt new methods. Is Canada adopting new methods similar to those to which I have referred? True, we have three ministers of defence; I think it is true also to say that the plebiscite bill recently passed was a defence measure- a defence of members of the government for their past performances. May we not learn from our enemies, who have introduced into this war entirely new tactics? Only to-day a Japanese general is reported on the radio to have said, "Defence methods will never lead to victory." I would1 addi that Australia did not hesitate to place her military forces under the command of a man of experience and proven ability, even to the extent of going to the United States to secure such a man, when they obtained General MacArthur. Mr. Churchill did not hesitate to go to Australia to secure a man militarily and diplomatically capable of filling a position in the middle east, when he appointed Hon. Richard Casey of Australia to that important post, at the same time making him a member of the British war cabinet.
I have just one more suggestion to make, which I have saved till the last because, in my opinion, it is the most important of all. I am sure no one will gainsay the truth of my assertion when I say that we have in Canada to-day a man who has the knowledge and experience, and who stands out as the greatest leader this country has ever produced. I refer to Lieutenant-General A. L. McNaughton, whom I now suggest that the Prime Minister appoint as minister of war and deputy prime minister. It may be urged that he could not be spared from his position overseas, but I venture the opinion that after two years of effort and training and planning, someone else could now be found to carry on his duties over there. I am sure that this would go a long way toward satisfying and relieving the anxious and much perturbed Canadian people.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in concluding his remarks last evening the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) sounded a very realistic note. While I do not agree with everything he said, I believe that his remarks in discussing many national problems should be carefully considered by every member of parliament. If there were other hon. members who felt disposed to follow along a similar line, I would hesitate to take the time of the house to say what I am going to say to-night.
The subject which I propose to discuss no doubt will appear to many hon. members as one which should be left until after the
war is over. I refer to the housing of the Canadian people, particularly those in our defence area. The hon. member for Park-dale (Mr. Bruce) made reference to the distinguished commander of the Canadian forces overseas. When General McNaughton was interviewed last fall by a delegation of Canadian editors and asked for a message which they could bring back to the Canadian people, which would convey to us the most urgent need of the moment, he is reported in an article written by Hugh Templin, which I believe appeared in most of the weekly newspapers of Ontario, as follows:
Asked what is the most urgent need at present, General McNaughton replied: Put every emphasis on the production of weapons and equipment. We need technical improvements such as can be worked out under the direction of the national research institute and others who work under Mr. Howe. Then these improvements must be put into production quickly. . . .
General McNaughton would not say how many should go into the army and how many into industry. 'We should survey our man-power first. We want no flash in the pan. We must plan for a w'ar of long duration and not put all our goods in the show window now.
I realize, Mr. Speaker, that the reverses have been many, and the thing that may impress many people at the moment as being most important may not necessarily be most important in the long run. I think that before Hitler will be defeated we must follow the suggestion of General McNaughton and prepare great quantities of the most modern equipment; and if that is to be done, the question I am now discussing becomes a matter of very great importance. Mr. Charles Abrams, in a recent copy of the New Republic, states.
. . . housing cannot win the war, but it can lose it. The habitats of thousands are now boxcars, pews, jails. Defence workers, bidding against each other, have doubled room rents and brought back the three-shift hot-bed. Increased rents have wiped out wage rises. Employers complain of labour turnover, inefficiency, disaffection; health officers warn of epidemics. Lack of housing has upset the production time table. Our programme of defence housing has failed; our wartime housing programme is threatened.
If all the workers in industry could live in surroundings similar to those enjoyed by members of parliament in Ottawa, there would be no question of our production being affected by housing. But in order that hon. members might understand the problems facing the workers, I would suggest that for the next three months we live on a budget similar to that followed by workers in industry, and then set out in this or any other city in Canada to find suitable housing for our families. In the city of Ottawa a great deal has been said
War Appropriation

about the difficulties experienced by stenographers who come here; and reliable reports indicate that already we are facing a very serious turnover of labour in all the cities of Canada where our large industries are located, as a result of workers being unable to secure housing. During the last war in the United States they found that in key industries they had a labour, turnover of from 100 to 1,000 per cent per annum, as a direct result of not being able to find houses for their people. In the production of munitions this year we shall spend at least a billion dollars; and for the . sake of argument assume that we may have a wastage of 10 per cent as a direct result of workers not being able to find living quarters. Thus, in terms of dollars and cents you have a wastage of $100,000,000.
Let me illustrate the problem that arises. In the city of Hamilton, for example, we have many of our largest war industries. Men have gone to that city from all parts of the dominion. Recently I visited one of my constituents who moved there. He spent days and days trying to find a place for himself, his wife and his family to live, and at last in desperation he bought a house for which he paid a cash payment of $300 and arranged to pay the balance in monthly payments representing about twice what that house was actually worth in terms of rental. In all probability this man will be leaving Hamilton when the war is over; but if he had not been in a position to pay the amount I mentioned, I do not know what he would have done for housing accommodation. He happens to be a trained artisan; but had he been unable to find housing in Hamilton, and if he could have found in Guelph or Palmerston or Georgetown a place to live, so that his children could go to school, naturally he would have left the essential war industry if he could have found any sort of employment, even in a non-essential industry.
I realize that the government has given consideration to this question. A year ago it was so impressed with the matter that $10,000,000 was appropriated to set up Wartime Housing; and at a later date, when the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) is in the house, I plan to say something about Wartime Housing projects. I o-night, however, I make a special plea to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley), before he writes finis to a very interesting chapter in housing in Canada, the national housing administration. Representations have been made to the Minister of Finance from many places in Canada appealing to him to have activities in connection with national housing

continued for at least another year. I know the problem confronting the minister in finding money, spending it, and satisfying the many demands. It might seem to him that this is a place where economy might be effected, and that we might discontinue the building of cheap permanent houses until the war is over. But let me remind the house of the condition which prevailed in Canada at the commencement of the war.
Canada and the United States had two of the most unenviable records, as far as providing houses within the range limit of people receiving low incomes is concerned. No civilized country in the world waited as long as we did, before giving consideration to this national problem. We have said that this was a problem for the municipalities. The municipalities have replied, "We cannot cope with it; the provinces should assume the responsibility." The provinces, in turn, pass the buck to the dominion.
In the time at my disposal, I am unable to review the development in Canada since 1913, when the very first Canadian conference ever to be held in connection with town planning was assembled in Winnipeg. I have before me a table showing the building activities in eighteen of the most important countries in the world between the years 1929 and 1937. Canada is outstanding in this report in two respects. Taking 1929 as a base period of 100, our percentage dropped to a level lower than that of any of the other countries-namely to a point of 9-7 in 1933. It remained at the lowest level in 1937, when it stood at 24. Other countries, such as Great Britain, did not get below 114 in 1933 and 151 in 1937. In Great Britain they took the attitude, quite correctly, "Here is a field where the government should spend a large sum of money. Money invested by a government in providing low-priced housing is a good investment." They realized that workers who otherwise would be unemployed would in this way be engaged in using raw materials to build something of permanent value. The result is that in the United Kingdom they had a comparatively good record.
If we take 1932 as a base period at 100, we find that the figure for south Africa in 1937 was 582, or five times as much building in 1937 as there was at the depth of the depression. Unfortunately statistics are not available for a very wide area in Canada. As a matter of fact, Winnipeg is the only city in Canada that has prepared a careful annual report which gives any true picture of the prevailing situation. The last report from Winnipeg points out that during the last five years the total dwellings and suites provided was 1,886, while

War Appropriation
during the same period there were 18,322 marriages, or one dwelling or suite for approximately every ten marriages. Of course, many of the marriages are of people from outside the city; but if three-fourths of the marriages were of city people, the rate would be only one dwelling or suite provided for approximately every seven marriages.
The figures show that in 1941 Winnipeg had the most serious housing shortage in its history. There were only 111 vacancies, including suites and houses, as compared with 337 in the previous year and 704 in the year before that. In other words, the vacancies amounted to less than one per cent. Last week the mayor of Winnipeg appeared in Ottawa with other mayors to present the housing problem to the Minister of Finance. AVhile here, he told me of some of the problems which arise in a city like Winnipeg. The wife of a man who is overseas had informed him she had been notified to vacate, and she had not the faintest idea where another house could be secured. He pointed out that this was very bad for the morale of our troops. It is not good to have married men in the forces learn that housing is not available for their dependents here, and that there will not be sufficient housing for them when the war is over.
I realize it is very important that our men and materials should be used in the production of those things which are most necessary. But we have in Canada a great many middle-aged men who have been associated with the building trades, and who will be in the ranks of the unemployed unless we continue our house building programme. I am referring to houses built under plans such as the national housing administration. Housing under Wartime Housing Limited is being carried on by large contractors, and the small contractor has not a chance to enter the picture at all. So, from the point of view of housing our people who are in war industries, and housing the relatives of our men in the forces, I suggest that the minister should give this problem very careful consideration before he dismisses it. I am sure it has been presented to him with great force by many delegations.
I do not approach the subject from the point of view of those real estate people who are concerned about the carrying on of a national housing activity from a purely personal point of view. I am thinking only in terms of a national problem. Again I must say that unless a maximum housing programme is carried on in Canada, we are going to have a very serious reduction in our production, and we shall have a whole host of social problems before the war is over, and after it.
I believe the national housing programme is one which might give the Minister of Finance a great measure of pride. I have in my hand pictures sent to me by the Quality Homes Corporation of Vancouver, showing homes which had been built in Vancouver under Wartime Housing Limited. As has been stated repeatedly, these houses are only temporary. Assurances have been given that they will be demolished- when the war is over. Wartime Housing Limited have been able to satisfy public opinion that these houses will not interfere with the investments of the other property owners. The houses built in Greater Vancouver by Wartime Housing Limited are built at an average cost of $2,996.97 per house, without basement or furnace. In the same city permanent houses have been built with full-sized basements, containing furnaces. These houses are of permanent construction, and they are built at a cost of $2,500, or approximately $500 per house less than these flimsy wartime houses.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF TRANSFER AGREEMENT RESPECTING ROYALTIES ON OIL PRODUCTION

speechtext:
Hon. T. A. CRERAR (Minister of Mines and Resources) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 18, to amend the Alberta Natural Resources Acts.
He said: In 1929, by agreement between the federal government and the province of Alberta, the natural resources in that province were transferred to the Alberta government. At that time there were certain licences outstanding for oil rights and timber rights. These licences had been issued by the federal government, and of course the Alberta government accepted the responsibilities which attached to the licences. Under the terms of the transfer agreement it was held that their conditions could not be varied. In 1938 it was necessary to amend the transfer agreement to enable the Alberta government to put into effect certain conservation measures in respect of the oil development in the Turner valley. The present amendment to the transfer agreement also relates to oil produced in Alberta. The Alberta government have been desirous for some time to secure the power to vary the royalties which may be charged. Certain wells were capable of paying higher royalties than other wells, but the government was limited to similar treatment for all wells covered by dominion licence. The matter has been the subject of discussion between the provincial authorities and the majority of those interested in the oil industry, and the amendment to the transfer agreement which is here proposed is to give effect to certain understandings which have been reached between the provincial government and these oil interests.

Subsequently that was done, and we were advised several weeks ago by representatives of the oil interests and by the province that they wished to have the agreement amended to give effect to certain understandings they had reached.

1.	As a result of approximately 1,800 surveys of machine shops alone, every effort has been made and is being made to bring all of the machine shops in Canada into war production, consistent with the efficiency required to make as much war material as possible, as soon as possible.
We are still in the position, partly due to shortages in raw materials, of being able to select first those machine shops which can be used most efficiently. This efficiency depends upon:
(i)	A combination of good management and skilled labour with machine tools which are in shape to do the precision work required in to-day's war machines;

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

speechtext: The house resumed from Tuesday, March 24, consideration of the motion of Mr. Usley that the house go into committee to consider a resolution to provide that sums not exceeding $135,000,000 be granted to his majesty for national defence and security.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before eleven o'clock last evening I was discussing a question which would have been left until after the Easter recess had it not been for the fact that unless something is done immediately in this connection the effect upon our production programme will be very serious indeed. I am referring, of course, to the question of wartime housing. Hon. members no doubt are aware of the fact that during the past year we have had two departments engaged in trying to provide more adequate housing in key centres in Canada. I refer to the activities of the national housing administration and to Wartime Housing Limited.
Last year I expressed the opinion that the entire programme of providing housing in war time should have been administered by the government owned and controlled agency, the national housing administration. The government, however, decided otherwise; and a number of dollar a year men were entrusted with the responsibility of administering Wartime Housing Limited. I do not plan to discuss their activities at this time, but after careful consideration and comparison of costs it would appear to me that we are getting permanent construction under national housing for less than we are getting temporary housing under Wartime Housing Limited. Last night I referred to a return which was tabled some time ago, giving the cost of war-time houses built in North Vancouver. It showed a striking discrepancy between the costs of

War Appropriation
war-time houses and those built under natonal housing in that city. I have -before me a return brought down on February 3 of this year, giving the average costs of these temporary houses in various cities, as follows:
Fort William	 $2,860
Halifax	  3,742
Hamilton	    2,818
Welland	 2,886
Peterborough	 3,018
Wrightville	 3,379
Let me remind hon. members that these houses are of temporary construction, without basements and without furnaces. The fuel is stored in a box, attached to the back of the house, capable of holding half a ton of coal. Some of the occupants of these houses in Hamilton spoke of the difficulties they experienced in securing fuel deliveries, since the box has to be empty before half a ton of coal can be put in, and there is an extra charge of fifty cents for making these small deliveries. In view of the fact that permanent houses have been built in many of these centres at much lower cost it does seem to me that it would be a great mistake to terminate the activities of the national housing administration. I understand that since the commencement of the war that agency has assisted in the construction of over 12,854 houses, at a cost to the treasury of Canada of approximately $9,700,000. I should like hon. members to remember these figures. According to the information given by the Minister of Munitions and Supply, we are committed to a spending programme of over $20,000,000 for something like six thousand houses, under the wartime housing programme. I know the answer will be given that these houses have to be built in a hurry, and that necessarily the cost is higher.

I would urge hon. members to go and see those houses, and then draw their own conclusions as to whether or not the taxpayers of Canada have received good value for the money that has been spent. What the minister says is true with regard to arrangements under
the national housing administration; but in Canada there are a great many cities which would be quite prepared to encourage the administration to undertake a building programme. Of course it must be remembered also that the figures I gave represented only the government's investment, not the total cost of those houses. The average cost of the permanent houses is given as $3,250. I think hon. members will agree that if permanent houses can be built for anything like the cost of the temporary houses, we should encourage the construction of permanent dwellings as far as possible at this time.
I realize that the whole question of supplies must be taken into consideration. It is quite conceivable that we may have to use very different methods of construction; that we may have to abandon the installation of bath tubs, and that houses may not be wired for electricity if the shortage of copper becomes more acute. We might even be required to get along without central heating. But I submit that the government should take into consideration the raw materials and manpower that will be available for the construction of permanent houses, so that the promise given by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) some time ago that we are not going to be governed by dollars and cents but that whatever is physically possible will be made financially possible, may be implemented. That policy should be carried out in connection with housing. It will be a great calamity if the national housing administration is compelled to fold up, with the personnel obliged to go into private industry or leave the country, so that the only building activity will be carried on by Wartime Housing Limited.
I should like to remind hon. members that it is estimated that ninety per cent of the 12,000 houses which have been built since the beginning of the war by the national housing administration have been constructed in centres where we consider there is a definite war-time housing shortage. According to the order in council which was passed when Wartime Housing was established, the places in which construction should be carried on were centres where the production of munitions of war and supplies, or defence projects, would be affected by the lack of housing. There are a great many places in Canada where training centres and military establishments are located to which men of the armed forces bring their families, and if it is physically possible we should be prepared to provide them with housing accommodation. I make this final plea to the government that it give the most careful consideration to providing an appropriation for national housing and that national housing be given consideration in the matter
War Appropriation

of priorities. It would be unfortunate if all the bathtubs, heating appliances and wiring were directed exclusively into wartime housing so that the national housing administration would find it impossible to carry on. I hope the government [DOT]will give careful consideration to the argument I have presented, so that our munitions production may not be seriously handicapped in the months to come because of adequate housing not being available.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to participate in this debate until the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) last evening brought out a circumstance which, I think, demands reiteration of the rights of parliament. Some time ago an address was delivered in this house by the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Moore) in reference to the like matter, in which he stressed the situation to-day prevailing in the parliament generally speaking, indicated the trend away from democratic practices. I find it hard to understand why so important a measure as the war appropriation should have been delayed in being brought down to the house until a day or so before the Easter recess. This is not the first time this has occurred. This is one measure that gives us as members an opportunity of placing our viewpoint before the house and the country and of obtaining information with regard to the position of our war effort. I cannot understand why a measure such as this should not have been introduced earlier in the session. Various explanations may be given, but the fact remains that in the last two or three days before the Easter recess we are asked to deal with an expenditure of many millions of dollars and to vote supply to enable the government to continue during the period of the Easter recess.

have been all right during the routine days of peace; but my submission is that with a war on-I reiterate what I have said before-committees of the private members of this house should be set up along the lines of the committees which the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) is having set up at the present time, to enable members to recommend to the government the cutting down of unnecessary expenditures because, Mr. Speaker, the thing the government should do to-day-and it would thereby secure the unanimous support of the country is to reduce non-war expenditures to the limit.
Donald Gordon, chairman of the wartime prices and trade board, speaking in the city of Montreal, outlined the position of Canada to-day and emphasized the necessity for action. He stressed the terrible urgency of the situation to-day and said:
Selfish or private interests must he ruled out completely. The competitive system must go, to be replaced with one which is based entirely upon the criterion of maximum production, with the most efficient use of labour, machinery and materials to operate steadily without cease except for necessary rest or maintenance.
Then he used these words:
Regimentation and more regimentation was coming for Canada, he continued, hut "let us develop it without the ugly meaning which it has been given in gestapo land and by the Japanese imitators."
He points out that regimentation is coming in ever-increasing measure. I realize, as all of us must, that during a period of war it is necessary that the freedoms, which are ordinarily accepted as inherent in democracy be controlled in the greater interest of the safety of the state-the freedom of the press, freedom of speech, freedom of association and the like. As Lord Baldwin said:
The price of liberty is eternal vigilance, eternal knowledge, eternal sympathy and eternal understanding.
In Great Britain the rights of parliament have been restricted as have the rights of individuals, the rights of the whole people throughout the nation; but, Mr. Speaker, they are doing it with the consent and under the control of parliament, and wherever there is an invasion of the rights normally enjoyed by the citizens of Great Britain the matter first comes before parliament and is debated. I point this out because the hon. member for Vancouver East last evening in his address showed that information, whatever its source may be, which is not being furnished to parliament, is being or has been furnished to private corporations. That is a flouting of the rights of the members of this house, but it is what has been going on in ever-increasing

War Appropriation
measure ever since the war began. I point out first the fact that until recently it was impossible for the members of any party other than the government party to go on the national radio network; yet day after day members of the government and members of its various boards are making speeches, many of them tinged by political considerations. It is through the instrumentality of the radio- and it is at least one of the main methods

that public opinion can be created to-day. The other method is through the press, and the government is trying to control the press. Prosecutions are taking place from time to time; and while up to date none of them has been successful, the fact remains that the taking of the prosecution, unjustified though it was proven subsequently by the finding of the court, has a tendency to restrict the freedom of the press.
I am not going into any detail, but I would point out the tendency on the part of this government to do that which has been condemned by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) over a period of years. I refer to the almost universal ruling by decree, by order in council. This has been so to such an extent that in May, 1941, the Prime Minister stated that statutes had been changed or suspended in their operations since the outbreak of the war, but that the government had no record of the statutes that had been so changed. So general has this trend become that statutes passed by this parliament, such as the War Exchange Conservation Act and the excess profits tax, now allow the governor in council to discriminate in favour of one individual as against another. In other words, the rule of law that provides for equality before the law and allows each and every citizen of this country an opportunity to take his case to establish that equality before the courts is denied, when in statutes we allow the government to suspend or amend them by order in council.
If we as a parliament continue to receive the answers that we have received during the last few days-this practice is ever-widening in its scope-we shall find ourselves, unless we protest, where the government will proceed to say to us, regardless of what the matter is which we ask about, that it is not in the public interest that information should be given. If our right to secure information is denied, we are meeting here as a parliament for one purpose only, to vote supply. Other than that there would be very little justification for our being here. Everything that we pass by way of law could be passed by the instrumentality of orders in council, and even
the few bills that do come before parliament appear to be merely fillers in between votes of supply and supply.
From time to time the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) has replied to questions about production in a way that I suggest is not considerate of the rights of parliament. It would appear that the answers were prepared by a bureaucracy, by the rule of desk, instead of by a responsible minister answerable to parliament. On February 6 I asked how many licences had been granted for the erection of buildings other than those required for war industry since construction control had been adopted. In other words,
I wanted to find out whether, during a time when all materials were required for war purposes, certain materials were being allocated for civilian or domestic purposes. The answer I received is a revelation of the attitude of certain bureaucrats to this parliament, the representatives of the people. The answer was as follows:
There have been issued up to February 5, 1942, a total of 3,150 licences for the erection of buildings. Records covering these do not differentiate between war and non-war industries. A clear line of demarcation is not possible.
Thaf means one of two things. Either the answer is evasive to conceal that permits are being given for non-essential purposes, or permits are being issued by the board in charge without regard to whether or not they are for war purposes.
I would direct attention to the answer given to-day by the Minister of Munitions and Supply to the effect that the British government does not want information given out. I realize that in connection with particulars of quantities and details of that kind, it might be dangerous to give out information-not one of us wants any such information. In a recent speech the minister said that we now can equip a division in six weeks, but when we want to cross-examine him and find out the production in order to ascertain whether that is a statement of fact or merely a statement to make us all feel good, we receive the answer that it would not be in the public interest to give the information.
True, it would not be in the public interest 'to give out information that might be helpful to the enemy, but I think that is an excuse which is being used by this government to an ever-increasing extent as a latch-key to shut the door against information. That is the attitude they are taking. We want information; we want particulars. If the particulars and information cannot be given to us in the house, then let it be given in a secret session. We are asked to look into the expenditures of
War Appropriation

millions of dollars, and yet no information is given to us except in general terms. We are asked to vote millions and billions of dollars when we realize, as do the people of Canada, that it is not expenditures of themselves that will preserve freedom; it is tike result that follows that will achieve its preservation.
What is being done with the money? Only a few short months ago the system that was followed previously of issuing monthly lists of contracts awarded was done away with. To-diay no member of this house, unless he is a member of the government, has any idea of what contracts 'have been let since (the issue of this information was discontinued. What expenditures have been made? Who have been the recipients of contracts in the different provinces? All we know is that money has been spent and no information has been given as to the nature and the particulars thereof or the results. The people are willing to sacrifice, but they want to know what use is being made of the money being expended.
Within the last few days a number of articles have appeared in the western press by Mr. Dexter, one of which was referred to the other evening by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green). In one of these articles Mr. Dexter discussed the whole production situation. We have had no information on this. No information is being brought before parliament." No information is being made available to parliament. This series of articles points out that we have not yet achieved all-out production in Canada, that we have not to-day a nearly all-out production. All we have in fact is promises of future action, of what will happen in 1943. This parliament representing the people of Canada is concerned with what is going to happen in 1942 and have the right to know the present position.
I think we have a right to know where we are going and what is the plan in reference to production. Can time run forever in our favour? The record in the far east in the last four or five months has been terrible in its implications. Defeats, glorious defeats; retreats, glorious retreats, all because of the fact that there has been a need, not of manpower with courage but of sufficient manpower; a need, not of proper machinery but of sufficient amounts of proper machinery.
To-day in this country there should be a stop to the construction of buildings for civilian purposes. It is not being stopped: the answer to which I referred a while ago shows this. Is it not about time that the increase of man-power in industry due to enlarged demands for civilian requirements should be restricted? Since the beginning of this war there has been an additional employ-
ment of one million men, of whom the increased demand for consumer goods accounts for 339,000. Why has this flow of consumer goods production not been stopped? The people are willing to accept a reduced standard of living; yet to-day we have more men producing goods for civilian and domestic uses than in 1939, and I would point out that one of the orders in council which the Prime Minister placed before parliament yesterday. starts with the admission that there is a shortage of man-power in the country for war and industrial purposes. I shall allude to that again in a moment. In the meanwhile let us see what this increased employment has, in large measure, done. Here are the comparative index figures showing the increases:

Trade	1939	1941Furniture	.. 84-2	118-4Musical instruments....	.. 59-9	86-1Beverages 	.. 181-8	235-2Heating appliances
